record.title: MolDesignBench reports persistent constraint and feasibility failures in molecular-design agents
record.summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces MolDesignBench, a benchmark of 2,000 small-molecule generation and optimization tasks. Tasks combine implicit narrative requirements with explicit chemical constraints, include infeasible specifications, and expose 17 chemistry tools. Across six general and chemistry-focused agent configurations, the authors report best success rates of 38% for generation and 43% for optimization. The benchmark tests constraint handling and tool use; it does not test experimental property measurements or whether generated molecules lead to discoveries.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint defines a benchmark with 2,000 small-molecule generation and optimization instances, a 17-tool interface, explicit and implicit constraints, and infeasible cases.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the best evaluated agent achieved 0.38 success on generation and 0.43 on optimization in their benchmark; tool access generally improved performance.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the reported tests, agents often missed implicit requirements and struggled to identify infeasible specifications; the paper reports large implicit-constraint error shares for some tested models.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study evaluates computationally predicted molecular properties in synthetic small-molecule tasks; it does not establish experimental properties, successful synthesis, or novel molecular discovery.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or audit of task construction, tool correctness, or the reported agent scores has been completed.
The relationship between benchmark scores and experimental molecular-design outcomes is unmeasured.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported benchmark exposes a durable gap in current chemical-agent evaluations, it can change how teams assess tool-using agents for molecular design and help prevent over-reading narrow chemistry scores. The consequence is meaningful within scientific-agent evaluation, not a claim of demonstrated drug discovery.
limitations: All benchmark outcomes are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced here.
The task set focuses on small molecules, not polymers, crystals or other chemical domains.
Molecular properties rely on computational predictions rather than experimental measurement; the benchmark does not establish synthesis or novel discovery.
Results are bounded to six tested agent configurations, this tool interface and the stated prompt/turn protocol; broader transfer is unknown.
The authors report the best success rate separately for generation and optimization, not a single aggregate score.
brief.summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces MolDesignBench, a benchmark of 2,000 small-molecule generation and optimization tasks. Tasks combine implicit narrative requirements with explicit chemical constraints, include infeasible specifications, and expose 17 chemistry tools. Across six general and chemistry-focused agent configurations, the authors report best success rates of 38% for generation and 43% for optimization. The benchmark tests constraint handling and tool use; it does not test experimental property measurements or whether generated molecules lead to discoveries.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report best success of 0.38 for molecule generation and 0.43 for optimization, with GPT-5.4 the strongest tested agent. Tool access generally raises scores; explicit presentation of constraints improves reported success and infeasibility detection. These are preprint results, not independently reproduced here.
technical.compute_or_cost: Not reported as a comparable deployment-cost study. The interaction protocol caps tasks at 20 assistant turns; tool calls are counted separately.
technical.demonstrated_result: The benchmark description, task schema, tool interface, evaluation protocol and reported tables are directly inspectable in the arXiv paper. Performance outcomes are labeled CLAIMED because they are author-run.
technical.implementation_status: The preprint describes a benchmark and linked public data/code artifacts; no deployed molecular-design system or experimental validation is established.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark generates molecular tasks from design-stage/strategy scenarios, embedding some property constraints in narrative text while also supplying explicit property or functional-group conditions. A 17-tool interface supports generation, analysis, retrieval, coding and molecular representation. The evaluation scores constraint satisfaction and infeasibility judgments.
technical.novelty: The benchmark combines scenario-embedded implicit requirements, multiple constraints, infeasible tasks and adaptive multi-turn chemistry-tool use in one evaluation setting.
technical.regime: Two tasks (generation and optimization), 1,000 instances each, 90% feasible and 10% infeasible; six general or chemistry-specialized agent configurations; up to 20 assistant turns per task; computational molecular-property estimates.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links a public dataset and author repository, but no independent reproduction was performed in this activation. Linked artifact landing pages were inspected, not executed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Table 3 compares six agent configurations with and without tool access: GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-235B, Ether0-24B and InternLM-S1-241B. No human expert performance baseline is reported in the main experiment.

brief.title: MolDesignBench reports persistent constraint and feasibility failures in molecular-design agents
brief.why_it_matters: The benchmark makes implicit constraints, conflicting requirements and infeasible requests part of a structured evaluation, areas that simpler chemistry tasks may not test. Its reported results suggest current agents can perform poorly even with specialized tools. This is useful evidence for evaluation design, while its synthetic small-molecule setting cannot establish real-world discovery performance.
